Concept. The critical section is a piece of code, not a piece of memory and not a phase of the process's life. It is the region that touches shared data, so concurrent execution of it by two processes would break mutual exclusion.

Step by step.

  1. A process alternates between its critical section and its remainder section.
  2. The critical section is defined by which shared variables it reads and writes, not by how long it runs.
  3. Because the shared data can be left inconsistent if two processes interleave inside that region, the protocol must allow at most one process inside at a time.
  4. That is exactly option (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) confuses the critical section with a start-up phase; every process may run for a long time before reaching its critical section.
  • (C) confuses code with the code segment of the address space.
  • (D) confuses the critical section with kernel memory.

Common misconception. Candidates read 'critical section' as 'the important part of the program'. It is defined purely by shared-data access.

Takeaway. Critical section = code that touches shared state. Mutual exclusion is required inside it and nowhere else.

questions.question: The instruction test-and-set(lock) is executed atomically by the hardware. Which one of the following does it do?
options: It reads the current value of lock, sets lock to true, and returns the value it read.
It sets lock to true and returns nothing.
It sets lock to false unconditionally.
It reads lock twice and returns the larger of the two values.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. test-and-set is a read-and-write pair that the hardware performs indivisibly. The value it returns is the old value, and the value it leaves behind is true. That combination is what makes a lock possible.

Step by step.

  1. The atomic action is: old = lock; lock = true; return old.
  2. If the returned old value is false, the caller has just taken the lock, because nobody else held it.
  3. If the returned old value is true, somebody else already held the lock, so the caller must retry.
  4. This is option (A).

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) loses the information the caller needs: without the old value the process cannot tell whether it acquired the lock.
  • (C) would release the lock rather than acquire it.
  • (D) is not an atomic read-modify-write at all.

Common misconception. The common error is to remember only that test-and-set 'sets the flag to true' and to forget that its return value is the previous flag.

Takeaway. test-and-set: returns the old value, leaves true behind. The returned value decides who got in.

questions.question: How does a binary semaphore differ from a counting semaphore?
options: A binary semaphore can take only the values 0 and 1, whereas a counting semaphore can take any non-negative integer value.
A binary semaphore cannot be used to provide mutual exclusion.
A binary semaphore never blocks the process that waits on it.
A counting semaphore cannot be implemented using binary semaphores.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Both kinds of semaphore support the same two operations, P (wait) and V (signal). They differ only in the range of values the counter may take.

Step by step.

  1. A binary semaphore's counter is confined to {0, 1}, so it behaves exactly like a mutex.
  2. A counting semaphore's counter may be any non-negative integer and therefore models a pool of N identical resources.
  3. Hence the distinction is the range of the counter, which is option (A).

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is false: the binary semaphore is the standard mutex.
  • (C) is false: P on a binary semaphore at 0 blocks exactly as it does on a counting semaphore.
  • (D) is false: a counting semaphore initialised to N can be built from N binary semaphores, and a general counting semaphore can be built from a binary semaphore plus a counter.

Common misconception. Students assume the binary semaphore is 'weaker'. It is not weaker — it is the same object restricted to two values.

Takeaway. Same operations, different counter range. Binary = mutex; counting = pool of resources.

questions.question: Which classic synchronisation problem is modelled by a fixed-size array into which producer processes insert items and from which consumer processes remove them?
options: The dining-philosophers problem
The readers–writers problem
The bounded-buffer (producer–consumer) problem
The sleeping-barber problem
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The bounded-buffer problem, also called the producer–consumer problem, is exactly this: a buffer of fixed capacity N, producers that insert while the buffer is not full, and consumers that remove while it is not empty.

Step by step.

  1. A producer must block when the buffer is full; that is the empty semaphore.
  2. A consumer must block when the buffer is empty; that is the full semaphore.
  3. Mutual exclusion on the buffer itself is the third semaphore, mutex.
  4. The description therefore matches option (C).

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is about five philosophers competing for forks.
  • (B) is about concurrent readers against an exclusive writer.
  • (D) is about a barber and a waiting-room of limited chairs.

Common misconception. The three classic problems look similar in a one-line summary. The distinguishing feature here is a fixed-capacity container.

Takeaway. Fixed-capacity container with inserters and removers = bounded buffer.

questions.question: A solution to the critical-section problem must satisfy three requirements. Which one of the following is NOT one of them?
options: Mutual exclusion
Progress
Bounded waiting
Absence of deadlock anywhere else in the system
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The three textbook requirements are mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. Deadlock freedom is a desirable property of the whole system, but it is not one of the three named requirements on the critical-section protocol itself.

Step by step.

  1. Mutual exclusion: at most one process is inside its critical section at a time.
  2. Progress: if no process is inside and some wish to enter, one of them must be admitted, and the choice cannot be postponed indefinitely by processes in their remainder sections.
  3. Bounded waiting: after a process has requested entry, there is a bound on how many times others may enter before it does.
  4. Deadlock freedom in the rest of the system is not among these three, so it is option (D).

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A), (B) and (C) are exactly the three requirements.

Common misconception. Candidates who have seen 'deadlock-free' used loosely about critical-section solutions pick (D) as if it were required.

Takeaway. Memorise the triple: mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting.

questions.question: A counting semaphore S is initialised to 3. The operations P, P, V, P, P, P, V, V, P are then executed in that order on a single semaphore, where P waits and V signals. The semaphore allows its value to become negative, and the magnitude of a negative value is then the number of processes blocked on it. What is the final value of S? (Enter an integer; it may be zero or negative.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A semaphore's value is simply incremented by V and decremented by P. A negative value is not an error: it records how many processes are waiting.

Step by step.

  1. Start: S = 3.
  2. P → 2; P → 1; V → 2; P → 1; P → 0; P → −1 (one process now blocked);
  3. V → 0 (the blocked process is woken, and the value returns to 0); V → 1; P → 0.
  4. Final value: S = 0.

Answer: 0.

Common misconception. The usual slip is to clamp the counter at 0 and then lose count of how many V operations were 'absorbed' by blocked processes.

Takeaway. Trace the counter one operation at a time and let it go negative; a V that wakes a sleeper restores the value to 0, not to 1.

questions.question: A spin lock is implemented with test-and-set. While one process is inside its critical section, what are the other processes that want the lock doing?
options: Sleeping in a blocked queue maintained by the kernel.
Repeatedly executing the test-and-set loop, consuming CPU time.
Waiting on a condition variable.
Nothing — they have been terminated.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A spin lock has no queue and no sleep. A waiting process keeps executing the acquire loop until the lock becomes free, so it burns CPU cycles for as long as it waits. This is why spin locks are useful only when the expected wait is shorter than two context switches.

Step by step.

  1. The acquire loop is while (test-and-set(lock));.
  2. While the lock is held, every iteration returns true and the loop repeats.
  3. No kernel structure records the waiter and no process is descheduled, so the CPU is spent spinning.
  4. This is option (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes a blocking lock built on semaphores or a mutex, not a spin lock.
  • (C) describes condition variables, which do suspend the waiter.
  • (D) is not a synchronisation behaviour at all.

Common misconception. The word 'wait' makes candidates picture a sleeping process. In a spin lock, waiting means running.

Takeaway. Spin lock = busy waiting: the waiter stays runnable and consumes the CPU.

questions.question: In the dining-philosophers problem with five philosophers seated around a circular table, how many forks must a philosopher hold in order to eat?
options: One
Two — the fork on the left and the fork on the right
Three
Five
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A philosopher needs both adjacent forks, which is what makes the problem interesting: the resources are shared between neighbours, so a philosopher can hold one fork and still be unable to proceed.

Step by step.

  1. Five forks are placed on the table, one between each pair of neighbouring philosophers.
  2. A philosopher can pick up only the two forks that are adjacent to their own place.
  3. Eating requires both, so two forks are needed.
  4. This is option (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the naive reading, but then no contention would arise and the problem would be trivial.
  • (C) and (D) exceed the two forks that are adjacent to any one philosopher.

Common misconception. The common mistake is to forget that the two forks are shared with the neighbours, which is the whole source of deadlock.

Takeaway. Two forks per philosopher, each shared with one neighbour — that sharing is the problem.

questions.question: A semaphore S has the value 4, and no process is blocked on it. A process now executes P(S). What is the new value of S, and what does the process do?
options: S becomes 5 and the process continues.
S becomes 3 and the process continues.
S becomes 3 and the process blocks.
S stays 4 and the process blocks.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. P(S) decrements the semaphore and blocks the caller only if the resulting value is negative. Decrementing 4 gives 3, which is not negative, so the process simply carries on.

Step by step.

  1. P(S): S ← S − 1.
  2. S becomes 3.
  3. Because the new value is ≥ 0, no resource shortage is implied and the caller is not blocked.
  4. This is option (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) increments, which is what V does.
  • (C) blocks even though the count is still positive.
  • (D) neither changes the count nor explains a block.

Common misconception. Some presentations describe P as 'wait until S > 0, then decrement'. Both descriptions agree here: 4 > 0, so the process decrements and proceeds.

Takeaway. P decrements and blocks only when the result goes negative; V increments and wakes one waiter.

questions.question: In Peterson's two-process solution, what is the role of the shared variable turn?
options: It records which process is currently inside its critical section.
It breaks the tie when both processes want to enter, by naming the process that must give way.
It counts how many times each process has entered its critical section.
It stores the other process's flag value.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each process raises its own flag to show that it wants in. If both flags are raised, the two are in conflict, and turn resolves it: the process that wrote turn last is the one that waits.

Step by step.

  1. Process i executes flag[i] = true; turn = j; and then waits while flag[j] && turn == j.
  2. If both set their flags, the later write to turn wins, so exactly one of them sees turn == j and defers.
  3. turn therefore decides who yields in the contested case, which is option (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is wrong: neither process sets turn on entering, and turn is meaningless once both flags are clear.
  • (C) is wrong: turn holds a process index, not a count.
  • (D) is wrong: each process reads the other's flag directly.

Common misconception. The tempting error is to think turn is a permission token that must be held. It is the opposite — it names the process that must step aside.

Takeaway. In Peterson's solution: flags say 'I want in'; turn says 'you go first'.

questions.question: The swap instruction used to build a lock is atomic. Which of the following is the correct acquire idiom?
options: key = true; do { swap(lock, key); } while (key); — the process enters when key is false.
key = false; do { swap(lock, key); } while (key == false); — the process enters when key is true.
swap(lock, key) is executed once, after which the lock is permanently held.
swap is used only to release the lock, never to acquire it.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. swap(lock, key) exchanges the two values atomically. Setting key = true first means that after the swap the lock is true and key holds whatever the lock used to be. A returned false means the lock was free and is now ours.

Step by step.

  1. Set key = true to express 'I want the lock'.
  2. Execute swap(lock, key): the lock becomes true and key receives the old lock value.
  3. If the old value was false, nobody held the lock and we now do — exit the loop.
  4. If the old value was true, somebody else holds it — loop and try again. That is option (A).

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) inverts the test, so it exits exactly when the lock is taken.
  • (C) ignores that the lock may already be held.
  • (D) is wrong: release is a plain store of false and needs no atomic instruction.

Common misconception. The direction of the flag is easy to get backwards. Fix it by asking what value must be in key for us to know we won: false.

Takeaway. Acquire with swap: load true into your key, swap, and win when you get false back.

questions.question: A counting semaphore S is initialised to 5. Exactly seven P(S) operations and four V(S) operations are then executed, in any order, and every one of them completes. What is the final value of S? (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The final value of a semaphore depends only on how many P and V operations were performed, never on their order, because each P subtracts one and each V adds one.

Step by step.

  1. Each P(S) subtracts 1 from S.
  2. Each V(S) adds 1 to S.
  3. Net change = −7 + 4 = −3.
  4. Final value = 5 − 3 = 2.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Order does matter for which processes block and for how long, but it never matters for the final count. Candidates sometimes try to trace an interleaving and lose track.

Takeaway. Final semaphore value = initial + (#V) − (#P). Order affects blocking, not the final count.

questions.question: In the producer–consumer problem with a bounded buffer of capacity N, which invariant must always hold?
options: full + empty = N
full − empty = N
full × empty = N
full = empty
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. full counts the items present and empty counts the free slots. Between them they always account for the whole buffer, so their sum is the capacity N at every instant.

Step by step.

  1. Initially full = 0 and empty = N, so the sum is N.
  2. A producer inserts an item: it decrements empty and increments full, so the sum is unchanged.
  3. A consumer removes an item: it increments empty and decrements full, again unchanged.
  4. The sum is therefore the invariant N, which is option (A).

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) would force full above N.
  • (C) is dimensionally meaningless here and fails for full = 0.
  • (D) would hold only for a half-full buffer.

Common misconception. Candidates confuse empty with 'the buffer is empty'. empty is a count of free slots, not a Boolean.

Takeaway. full = items present, empty = slots free, and they always sum to N.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about semaphores are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: P(S) decrements S and blocks the caller if the resulting value is negative.
V(S) increments S and wakes a blocked process if any is waiting.
A binary semaphore can be used to provide mutual exclusion.
A counting semaphore initialised to 1 always allows two processes into the critical section at the same time.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The two operations are duals: P consumes one unit of a resource and blocks when none is left, V returns one unit and wakes a waiter if there is one.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is the definition of P, including the blocking rule when the count goes negative.
  2. (B) is the definition of V, including the wake-up rule.
  3. (C) is true: a binary semaphore restricted to {0, 1} is exactly a mutex.
  4. (D) is false: a counting semaphore initialised to 1 admits one process; a second process blocks until the first signals.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. (D) is the trap: initialising a counting semaphore to 1 makes it behave as a binary semaphore, which excludes a second process, not one that admits two.

Takeaway. P blocks when the count would go negative; V wakes one waiter. An initial value of 1 means one process at a time.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about test-and-set based locks are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: test-and-set must be executed atomically by the hardware for the lock to be correct.
A plain test-and-set lock guarantees bounded waiting by itself.
A test-and-set lock makes waiting processes busy-wait, consuming CPU cycles.
On a uniprocessor, a spin lock held by a process that has just been preempted can waste an entire time quantum.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Atomicity gives mutual exclusion; it does not give fairness. Bounded waiting needs an ordering rule on top of the atomic primitive.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: if the read and the write could be interleaved, two processes could both observe false and both enter.
  2. (B) is false: the hardware primitive has no notion of arrival order, so a process can be overtaken arbitrarily many times.
  3. (C) is true: the waiter stays runnable and re-executes the acquire loop.
  4. (D) is true: the holder cannot run because the spinner has the CPU, so the quantum can be wasted before the holder ever releases the lock.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. (B) is the standard confusion: atomicity is not fairness. A test-and-set lock is correct but not starvation-free.

Takeaway. Atomic primitive gives mutual exclusion; add a queue or an ordering rule to get bounded waiting.

questions.question: A producer–consumer system uses a bounded buffer of capacity 9 together with the counting semaphores full and empty. At some instant full = 4 and no producer is blocked. How many further items can be inserted before a producer blocks? (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The number of free slots is empty, and empty = capacity − full.

Step by step.

  1. Capacity N = 9.
  2. full = 4, so 4 slots are occupied.
  3. Free slots = 9 − 4 = 5, and this equals the current value of empty.
  4. Each insertion consumes one free slot, so 5 more insertions are possible before empty reaches 0 and the next producer blocks.

Answer: 5.

Common misconception. Candidates sometimes answer 4, reading full as the number of free slots. full is the number of items present.

Takeaway. empty = N − full is the number of insertions still possible.

questions.question: Two processes share two counting semaphores A and B, both initialised to 1. Process P1 executes P(A); P(B); and process P2 executes P(B); P(A);. Which of the following can happen?
options: Nothing can go wrong, because semaphores prevent every synchronisation hazard.
A deadlock: P1 may hold A and wait for B while P2 holds B and waits for A.
Only a livelock, never a deadlock.
Both processes proceed, because counting semaphores are re-entrant.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Semaphores enforce mutual exclusion on each resource individually. They say nothing about the order in which a process acquires several resources, and that is exactly the circular-wait condition for deadlock.

Step by step.

  1. Suppose P1 completes P(A) and is preempted; A is now 0 and P1 holds it.
  2. P2 completes P(B); B is now 0 and P2 holds it.
  3. P1 now waits on B, held by P2; P2 now waits on A, held by P1. Each waits for a resource the other holds.
  4. This is a circular wait, so the system deadlocks. Option (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is false: semaphores protect each resource, not the acquisition sequence.
  • (C) is false: the processes are blocked, not spinning.
  • (D) is false: semaphores are not re-entrant in this sense, and P(B) by P1 simply blocks.

Common misconception. Candidates believe 'we used semaphores, so we are safe'. Mutual exclusion and deadlock freedom are different properties.

Takeaway. Deadlock is avoided by imposing a global order on resource acquisition, not by using semaphores correctly one at a time.

questions.question: A lock is acquired with key = true; do { swap(lock, key); } while (key);, where swap(a, b) exchanges two variables atomically and lock is initially false. Three processes attempt to acquire the lock one after another and none of them ever releases it. How many of the three swap calls leave true in the caller's key? (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. swap(lock, key) makes lock equal to the caller's key (true) and gives the caller the lock's previous value. A returned true therefore means the lock was already held.

Step by step.

  1. Process 1: key = true, lock = false. After swap, lock = true and key = false. One call returned false.
  2. Process 2: key = true, lock = true. After swap, lock = true and key = true. Returned true.
  3. Process 3: identical to process 2, because the lock was never released. Returned true.
  4. Two of the three calls leave true in key.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Candidates count the first call as returning true because the lock 'became true'. The relevant value is the one handed back to the caller, which is the old lock.

Takeaway. In a swap lock, the value you get back is the old lock: false means you won, true means keep spinning.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Peterson's two-process solution are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: It guarantees mutual exclusion.
It guarantees progress.
It guarantees bounded waiting.
It requires the flag[] array and turn to be updated together as one atomic step.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Peterson's solution satisfies all three critical-section requirements using only single-word reads and writes, which is what makes it remarkable — it needs no special hardware instruction.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Mutual exclusion: if both are inside, both must have read turn as the other's index, which is impossible because turn holds one value.
  2. (B) Progress: a process in its remainder section has its flag clear, so it cannot block the other.
  3. (C) Bounded waiting: once a process raises its flag, the other can enter at most once before it does.
  4. (D) is false: only individual reads and writes of flag[i] and turn need be atomic; the updates are separate statements.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. (D) is the trap. Peterson's solution is prized precisely because it needs no atomic read-modify-write of several variables — only atomic single-variable access.

Takeaway. Peterson's solution: three requirements met with ordinary reads and writes, no hardware primitive.

questions.question: A proposed critical-section protocol satisfies mutual exclusion and progress, but a process that has announced its intention may be overtaken arbitrarily many times before it finally enters. Which requirement does the protocol violate?
options: Mutual exclusion
Progress
Bounded waiting
Atomicity of the entry code
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Bounded waiting is precisely the guarantee that, after a process requests entry, there is a limit on how many times other processes may enter ahead of it. A protocol that lets others overtake without limit violates it while still keeping mutual exclusion and progress.

Step by step.

  1. Mutual exclusion is stated to hold.
  2. Progress is stated to hold, so someone is always admitted when the section is free.
  3. Unbounded overtaking is the definition of a violation of bounded waiting.
  4. The answer is option (C).

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (B) are explicitly given as satisfied.
  • (D) is a property of the implementation, not one of the three requirements, and nothing in the statement suggests it fails.

Common misconception. Bounded waiting and progress sound similar. Progress is about the system always making some progress; bounded waiting is about a particular process eventually getting its turn.

Takeaway. Progress = someone gets in. Bounded waiting = you get in after a bounded number of others.

questions.question: A binary semaphore mutex is initialised to 1 and used to protect a critical section. A process enters the critical section and, before leaving, executes P(mutex) a second time. What is the result?
options: It enters the critical section a second time, since binary semaphores are re-entrant.
It blocks on itself and the system deadlocks, because the value is already 0 and no other process can ever signal it.
The value of mutex becomes 2.
The kernel detects the error and terminates the process.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A binary semaphore has no notion of an owner, so the second P is treated as an ordinary request by a stranger. The value is already 0, so the process blocks on a resource that only it could release.

Step by step.

  1. On entry the process executed P(mutex), taking the value from 1 to 0.
  2. The second P(mutex) decrements 0 to −1 and blocks the caller.
  3. The only process that could execute V(mutex) to release it is the one now blocked.
  4. The process waits for itself: a self-deadlock. Option (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is false: semaphores are not re-entrant; recursive mutexes are a different construct and must be requested explicitly.
  • (C) is false: P decrements, it never increments.
  • (D) is false: the kernel does not police the user's protocol.

Common misconception. Candidates assume that because the process already 'owns' the lock, the second P is a no-op. A semaphore records a count, not an owner.

Takeaway. Re-entering a non-recursive mutex self-deadlocks. Ownership is a mutex concept, not a semaphore concept.

questions.question: Seven philosophers sit around a circular table with seven forks, one between each pair of neighbours. Each philosopher needs both adjacent forks in order to eat. Using the asymmetric solution, in which one designated philosopher picks up the right fork first while every other philosopher picks up the left fork first, what is the maximum number of philosophers that can be eating at the same time? (Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each eating philosopher occupies two forks, and every fork sits between exactly two philosophers, so at most ⌊7/2⌋ = 3 can eat at once. The asymmetric rule guarantees that this maximum is actually reachable without deadlock.

Step by step.

  1. There are 7 forks and each eating philosopher needs 2 distinct forks.
  2. Forks are never shared between two eating philosophers, so the number eating is at most ⌊7 / 2⌋ = 3.
  3. That bound is achievable: philosophers 1, 3 and 5 can hold forks (7,1), (2,3) and (4,5) respectively, and none of them blocks the others.
  4. The asymmetric rule removes the circular wait, so this configuration is actually reached. Answer: 3.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Candidates often answer 7, thinking every philosopher can hold one fork simultaneously — but holding one fork is not eating.

Takeaway. Maximum simultaneous eaters = ⌊forks / 2⌋; the asymmetric (hierarchy) rule only makes that maximum reachable without deadlock.

questions.question: In the first readers–writers solution, in which readers are never made to wait, what is the main hazard?
options: Readers can starve.
Writers can starve, because a continuous stream of readers keeps the resource occupied.
A reader and a writer can be inside the critical section at the same time.
Two readers can deadlock against each other.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The first readers–writers solution gives readers priority: a reader waits only while a writer is actually writing. If new readers keep arriving, the count of active readers never falls to zero, so a waiting writer is never admitted.

Step by step.

  1. A writer waits until the reader count reaches 0.
  2. Every arriving reader increments the count without regard to waiting writers.
  3. If readers arrive faster than the existing ones leave, the count never reaches 0.
  4. The writer therefore waits indefinitely: writer starvation. Option (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the hazard of the second (writer-priority) solution.
  • (C) is prevented by the semaphores in both solutions.
  • (D) is impossible: readers never block one another in this solution.

Common misconception. The two readers–writers solutions have mirror-image starvation hazards. Read the priority direction carefully before answering.

Takeaway. First solution → writers starve. Second solution → readers starve.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the classic synchronisation problems and their semaphore solutions are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: In the bounded-buffer problem, full is initialised to 0 and empty to the buffer capacity.
In the dining-philosophers problem, the simple solution in which every philosopher picks up the left fork first can deadlock.
In the readers–writers problem, several readers may read at the same time, but a writer needs exclusive access.
A counting semaphore cannot be used in a solution to the dining-philosophers problem.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each classic problem has a standard initialisation and a standard failure mode; knowing both is what the examiner tests.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: at the start the buffer holds nothing, so full = 0, and all N slots are free, so empty = N.
  2. (B) is true: if all five pick up their left fork simultaneously, each holds one fork and each waits for the right one, held by a neighbour — a circular wait.
  3. (C) is true: readers do not modify the data, so they can share; a writer must exclude everyone.
  4. (D) is false: a common fix uses a counting semaphore of 4 (or one binary semaphore per fork) to admit at most four philosophers at once.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. (D) is the trap. The dining-philosophers problem is solved with semaphores all the time; what fails is the naive ordering, not the primitive.

Takeaway. Know the initialisation and the failure mode of each classic problem; the fix is almost always a constraint on ordering or on the number admitted.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about hardware synchronisation primitives are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: test-and-set and swap are both atomic hardware instructions from which a mutual-exclusion lock can be built.
compare-and-swap returns the old value of a memory location and writes the new value only if the old value still equals an expected value.
Bounded waiting cannot be obtained from a bare test-and-set lock without adding a queue or an explicit ordering rule.
A test-and-set lock never causes a context switch while a process is spinning.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Hardware gives atomicity, not policy. Every fairness guarantee must be layered on top of the atomic primitive by software.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: both are single atomic read-modify-write instructions and each is enough to build a correct lock.
  2. (B) is the definition of compare-and-swap: it succeeds only if the value has not changed since it was read.
  3. (C) is true: the primitive has no record of who arrived first, so overtaking is unbounded unless a queue or ticket scheme is added.
  4. (D) is false: a spinning process stays runnable and can be preempted by the scheduler like any other.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. (D) is the trap. Spinning does not disable preemption; the spinner can be switched out at any time, and on a uniprocessor the lock holder may then be unable to run.

Takeaway. Atomicity from hardware; fairness from software. A spin lock is correct but not fair.

questions.question: Peterson's two-process solution needs shared data between the two processes. Which one of the following is exactly the shared data it uses?
options: Two boolean flags flag[0], flag[1] plus one integer variable turn.
One integer variable turn only, shared by both processes.
A single boolean lock variable that both processes test and set.
One integer per process, holding the identity of the process that is inside the critical section.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Peterson's solution combines a per-process declaration of intent with a single tie-breaking variable.

Step by step.

  1. Each process owns one boolean, flag[i], which it sets to true on entering the entry section and clears on leaving the exit section.
  2. The single integer turn records which of the two processes has the right of way when both want to enter.
  3. No other variable is read or written, so the shared state is exactly the two flags and turn.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is the strict-alternation protocol, which uses only turn and therefore violates progress.
  • (C) is a test-and-set lock, a hardware-primitive solution rather than Peterson's algorithm.
  • (D) describes an 'owner' variable, which Peterson's algorithm does not need because mutual exclusion follows from the flags together with turn.

Common misconception. Students remember 'Peterson uses turn' and forget the flag array; without the flags the algorithm cannot express that a process is interested.

questions.question: Which one of the following states the bounded-waiting requirement on a critical-section solution?
options: At most one process may be executing inside its critical section at any instant.
If no process is inside its critical section, a process that wishes to enter must be allowed to do so without being delayed by processes in their remainder sections.
There must be a limit on the number of times other processes may enter their critical sections after a given process has requested entry and before that request is granted.
Every process must eventually terminate after a finite number of critical-section entries.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Bounded waiting is a fairness condition, not a safety condition.

Step by step.

  1. Mutual exclusion bounds how many processes may be inside at once; progress says the choice of the next entrant cannot be postponed indefinitely.
  2. Bounded waiting adds a counting guarantee: once process Pi has announced its request, only a bounded number of other entries may occur before Pi is admitted.
  3. That is what prevents a fast process from overtaking a slow one arbitrarily many times.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is mutual exclusion.
  • (B) is progress.
  • (D) is a liveness property of the process, not of the entry protocol.

Common misconception. Progress and bounded waiting are often treated as one idea. Progress forbids indefinite postponement in the aggregate; bounded waiting forbids an unbounded number of overtakings of one specific requester.

questions.question: Two processes P0 and P1 use Peterson's solution. Initially flag[0] = flag[1] = false and turn = 0. The entry sections are then interleaved exactly as follows: P0 executes flag[0] = true and then turn = 1; next P1 executes flag[1] = true and then turn = 0. Both now evaluate their spin conditions. Which process enters the critical section first?
options: P0, because turn = 0 at the moment the tests are made.
P1, because it was the last process to write turn.
Both enter, so this interleaving breaks mutual exclusion.
Neither enters; each waits for the other and the two processes deadlock.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The spin condition of Pi is flag[j] && turn == j; the process with turn != j proceeds.

Step by step.

  1. After the interleaving, flag[0] = flag[1] = true and turn = 0.
  2. P0 tests flag[1] && turn == 1: flag[1] is true but turn is 0, so the condition is false and P0 leaves the loop.
  3. P1 tests flag[0] && turn == 0: both parts are true, so P1 keeps spinning.
  4. P0 therefore enters first, and P1 enters only after P0 clears flag[0] on exit.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the meaning of turn: the last writer yields, it does not win.
  • (C) and (D) cannot happen here because exactly one of the two conditions evaluates to true when both flags are set.

Common misconception. It is tempting to read turn = 0 as 'P0's turn to wait'. In Peterson's algorithm the process that writes turn = j is offering the other one priority.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the three requirements on a critical-section solution are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Mutual exclusion forbids two processes from executing inside their critical sections at the same time.
Progress forbids a process that wants to enter from being delayed indefinitely by processes that are in their remainder sections.
Bounded waiting limits the number of other processes' entries that may intervene between a request and the granting of that request.
A protocol that satisfies progress necessarily satisfies bounded waiting.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The three requirements are independent: a protocol can satisfy any two of them and fail the third.

Step by step.

  1. Mutual exclusion is the safety property: at most one process inside at any instant.
  2. Progress is a liveness property about the decision: if the critical section is free, only processes that are actually trying to enter may take part in choosing the next entrant, and that choice cannot be postponed for ever.
  3. Bounded waiting is a per-process fairness property: after a request is made, a finite bound applies to the number of intervening entries by others.
  4. Progress constrains the group, not the individual, so it cannot imply a per-process bound.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (D) is the classic confusion: a protocol can guarantee that somebody always enters (progress) while letting one unlucky process be overtaken indefinitely.

Common misconception. Progress and bounded waiting are routinely merged into one 'no starvation' idea. Starvation-freedom for an individual process is bounded waiting; progress is only the guarantee that the decision procedure keeps working.

questions.question: Which of the following pairings of a protocol with a requirement it fails are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A protocol that guarantees mutual exclusion is thereby guaranteed to guarantee progress as well.
Strict alternation using a single shared turn variable, where Pi enters only while turn != i, violates progress.
A bare test-and-set lock with no queue and no ordering rule violates bounded waiting.
Peterson's two-process solution satisfies mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each requirement is a separate obligation, and each of these three protocols fails exactly one of them.

Step by step.

  1. Strict alternation: if P1 is in its remainder section, P0 cannot enter twice in a row, although the critical section is free. That is a failure of progress, not of mutual exclusion.
  2. A bare test-and-set lock: a process that releases the lock can immediately re-acquire it, so another waiting process may be overtaken arbitrarily many times. Mutual exclusion and progress both hold; bounded waiting does not.
  3. Peterson's algorithm satisfies all three for two processes: the flags give mutual exclusion, turn guarantees that one of the two must proceed, and a waiting process can be overtaken at most once.
  4. Statement (A) is false because mutual exclusion says nothing about whether the next entrant is ever chosen.

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the pairing to reject: mutual exclusion is a safety property and implies no liveness property at all.

Common misconception. Candidates often mark strict alternation as correct because it 'looks like' a working protocol. It protects the shared data perfectly; what it destroys is the ability of one process to use a free critical section.

questions.question: Peterson's two-process solution is implemented on a modern multicore processor with per-core store buffers, and no memory barriers are emitted. It can fail to provide mutual exclusion because:
options: the spin loop while (flag[j] && turn == j); can never terminate on a processor that caches flag[j].
an integer variable cannot be written atomically, so turn may be torn between the two writers.
the compiler is allowed to hoist the load of flag[j] out of the loop, and that alone destroys the proof of mutual exclusion.
the store to flag[i] and the store to turn may become visible to the other core in an order different from program order, so each process can read a value of turn that lets it in.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Peterson's correctness argument assumes sequential consistency: that all processes observe every store in one common order.

Step by step.

  1. The proof relies on the fact that the write to turn by one process is seen by the other before that other process reads it.
  2. With a store buffer, the write to flag[i] can still be pending when turn = j becomes visible; the other core then sees the flag as false, skips the spin, and both processes enter.
  3. The cure is a memory barrier (or a release/acquire fence) between the two stores, not a change of algorithm.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the opposite failure — a stale cached value would make a process spin longer, not enter wrongly.
  • (B) is false: an aligned 32-bit integer store is atomic; tearing is not the issue here.
  • (C) is a real hazard on a uniprocessor with an optimising compiler, but it produces a stuck loop rather than two processes inside the critical section, and a barrier at the loop fixes it.

Common misconception. The textbook algorithm is correct on a sequentially consistent machine. On real hardware the atomicity of individual stores is not enough; the ordering between them is what the proof needs.

questions.question: Peterson's solution generalises to n processes using n - 1 levels, level 1 being the outermost, with one turn variable per level. A process must pass through every level before it may enter its critical section. For n = 6, through how many levels must a process pass?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The n-process generalisation replaces the single turn with one variable per level and makes every process climb all levels.

Step by step.

  1. Level k is entered by announcing interest and then setting the level's turn variable to the process's own index.
  2. A process leaves a level only when no other process is interested in that level, or when the level's turn variable no longer names it.
  3. There are n - 1 levels in total, and the critical section sits above the last one.
  4. For n = 6: 6 - 1 = 5 levels.

Answer: 5.

Common misconception. Answering n (6) by counting processes instead of levels, or n - 2 by forgetting that level 1 is used.

questions.question: A spin lock differs from a blocking mutex in the way a waiting process behaves. Which one of the following describes the spin lock's waiter?
options: It is placed on a queue and descheduled by the kernel until the lock is released.
It repeatedly executes the acquire instruction on the processor until the lock becomes free.
It cannot be preempted once it has started waiting.
It consumes no processor time while it waits.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A spin lock trades processor cycles for the absence of a context switch.

Step by step.

  1. The acquire step is a short loop around an atomic instruction, for example while (test_and_set(&lock)) ;.
  2. The waiter stays runnable and keeps executing that loop, so it is burning a processor rather than sleeping.
  3. A blocking mutex instead moves the waiter to a wait queue and wakes it on release, which costs two context switches but frees the processor.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes a blocking mutex, not a spin lock.
  • (C) is false: a spinning process can be preempted at any time.
  • (D) is the opposite of what spinning does.

Common misconception. The word 'wait' suggests the process is idle. A spinning process is fully active and competes for the CPU with everyone else.

questions.question: On a uniprocessor, spinning on a lock is a poor choice when the critical section is long. Which one of the following is the correct reason?
options: The spinning process keeps the processor busy, and the process that holds the lock cannot run until the spinner's time quantum ends.
The instruction test-and-set is not available on uniprocessors.
Spin locks cannot enforce mutual exclusion when there is only one processor.
The lock variable lives in a register and is lost at a context switch.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. On one processor, spinning and holding are mutually exclusive uses of the only CPU.

Step by step.

  1. If the lock holder has been preempted, it cannot make progress until it is scheduled again.
  2. A spinner that keeps its quantum runs the acquire loop for the whole quantum, so the holder waits at least that long.
  3. A blocking mutex puts the waiter to sleep, which lets the holder run immediately; that is why spin locks are recommended only for very short critical sections or for multiprocessors.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) and (C) are false: atomic test-and-set exists and mutual exclusion works on a uniprocessor.
  • (D) is false: the lock is a memory word, not a register.

Common misconception. Spin locks are not 'wrong' on a uniprocessor, just wasteful; the loss is bounded-waiting time, not correctness.

questions.question: The instruction fetch-and-add(X, 1) atomically returns the old value of X and then increments X. A ticket lock gives each arriving process the ticket returned by fetch-and-add on a counter, and lets the process proceed when a separate now-serving counter reaches its ticket. Compared with a bare test-and-set lock, the ticket lock additionally guarantees:
options: freedom from busy waiting, because a waiting process is descheduled.
atomicity of the critical section itself, not merely of the acquire step.
bounded waiting, because the lock is granted in the order in which tickets were taken.
that no memory barrier is needed on a multicore machine.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A ticket lock adds a queue implicitly: the ticket number is the position in that queue.

Step by step.

  1. Each arrival obtains a distinct ticket, so the arrival order is recorded in the counter itself.
  2. The release increments the now-serving counter, which hands the lock to exactly one ticket holder — the next in order.
  3. Because a process can be overtaken only by the processes already ahead of it in the queue, the number of intervening entries is bounded by the number of earlier arrivals.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is false: a ticket lock still spins.
  • (B) is false: atomicity of the acquire is what test-and-set already gives.
  • (D) is false: a ticket lock still needs fences to order the critical-section accesses around the acquire and release.

Common misconception. Every lock built from an atomic instruction gives mutual exclusion; what separates them is fairness. test-and-set gives none, ticket locks give FIFO order.

questions.question: Each statement below is about an atomic hardware primitive. Which of them are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The atomicity of test-and-set and swap is provided by the memory system, so no interleaving of two processors can occur inside one such instruction.
A spin lock avoids the overhead of a context switch but consumes processor cycles while it waits.
A single atomic instruction can update two unrelated memory words indivisibly.
compare-and-swap can implement both a lock and a lock-free counter, because it writes only when the observed value is still the expected one.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Atomic instructions move the mutual exclusion down into the hardware for one word at a time.

Step by step.

  1. test-and-set and swap are executed as indivisible read-modify-write cycles on the memory bus, which is why they cannot be interleaved.
  2. The trade-off of spinning is explicit: no context switch, but the waiting processor is busy.
  3. compare-and-swap returns the old value and stores only if it still equals the expected value, which is exactly what both a lock and a lock-free increment need.
  4. One instruction operates on one memory word; protecting a multi-word invariant still needs a lock or a transactional mechanism.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) is the statement to reject: atomicity is per memory location, not across two independent locations.

Common misconception. It is easy to over-read 'atomic': the guarantee covers a single word. Two counters updated by two atomic instructions are not jointly atomic.

questions.question: A lock is acquired with while (test_and_set(&lock)) ; and released with lock = false;. On a multicore machine with per-core store buffers, mutual exclusion can break down unless memory barriers are used. Which one of the following is the correct explanation?
options: test-and-set is not atomic when more than one processor executes it.
the release store may be reordered with the critical-section accesses, so another processor can observe the lock as free while the critical-section writes are still pending in the buffer.
the compiler removes the empty body of the loop, so the lock is never tested.
the lock variable must be declared volatile for the instruction itself to remain atomic.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The release is a store, and a store can be delayed behind other stores.

Step by step.

  1. Inside the critical section the holder writes shared data; those writes may sit in its store buffer.
  2. The release writes lock = false to the same buffer. Without a fence the two writes can reach memory out of order, so a second core sees the lock free and enters while the first core's data writes are still invisible.
  3. A release barrier before the unlock store, and an acquire barrier after the successful test-and-set, restore the ordering the algorithm assumes.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is false: test-and-set is atomic per memory operation.
  • (C) would produce a non-terminating loop, not two processes inside the critical section.
  • (D) is false: volatile prevents some compiler optimisations but does not order memory operations on the hardware.

Common misconception. Atomicity of each instruction is not the same as ordering between instructions. Most real spin-lock bugs on multicore machines are ordering bugs.

questions.question: A single test-and-set lock is contended by 8 processes. While exactly one of them is inside its critical section, what is the maximum number of processes that can be spinning on that lock at the same instant?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The lock is a single word with two values, so at most one holder and every other contender spins.

Step by step.

  1. The process that succeeded in test-and-set holds the lock and is inside the critical section.
  2. Every other contending process fails the test, sees the lock busy, and repeats the loop.
  3. With 8 contenders and one holder, at most 8 - 1 = 7 are spinning.

Answer: 7.

Common misconception. Answering 8 by counting every contender, including the holder, as a spinner.

questions.question: A counting semaphore S has the value 0 and no process is blocked on it. A process now executes P(S). Which one of the following is the outcome under the convention in which a negative value counts the blocked processes?
options: S remains 0 and the calling process continues into its critical section.
S becomes 1 and the calling process continues.
The calling process is terminated because the semaphore is exhausted.
S becomes −1 and the calling process blocks.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. P decrements first and only then decides whether the process may continue.

Step by step.

  1. The decrement takes S from 0 to −1.
  2. A negative value means the resource is over-committed, so the calling process is added to the semaphore's wait queue.
  3. The magnitude, 1, records that one process is now waiting; a later V(S) will return S to 0 and wake it.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) would be right only if the value had been positive before the decrement.
  • (B) reverses the direction of P.
  • (C) describes no semaphore semantics at all.

Common misconception. The test is 'was the value positive before the decrement', not 'is the value positive after it'. Decrement-then-test is what makes the negative value meaningful.

questions.question: A counting semaphore S has the value −2, with two processes blocked on it. A process executes V(S). What is the result?
options: S becomes −1 and exactly one blocked process is woken.
S becomes −3 and one more process is added to the wait queue.
S becomes 0 and both blocked processes are woken.
S becomes −1 and both blocked processes are woken.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. V increments the value and hands the resource to one waiter if there is one.

Step by step.

  1. The increment takes S from −2 to −1.
  2. Because waiters exist, the increment is immediately consumed: one process is removed from the queue and resumed.
  3. The remaining −1 records that one process is still waiting.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the direction of V.
  • (C) would require two increments.
  • (D) wakes too many waiters for a single V.

Common misconception. One V wakes one waiter. Waking all of them, as in a broadcast, is a different operation and is not what V means.

questions.question: A counting semaphore used to control access to 5 identical printers is initialised to 5. At some instant its value is −2, under the convention in which a negative value counts the blocked processes. How many processes are blocked on the semaphore at that instant?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Under the negative-value convention the magnitude of the value is exactly the length of the wait queue.

Step by step.

  1. The semaphore started at 5, one permit per printer.
  2. Each blocked process contributes 1 to the negative part of the value.
  3. The value is −2, so |−2| = 2 processes are waiting for a printer.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Reporting 5 − 2 = 3 by treating the value as a count of free printers; a negative value counts waiters, not permits.

questions.question: Three processes share a binary semaphore mutex initialised to 1. Process A is inside its critical section, having executed P(mutex). Processes B and C now both execute P(mutex) and block. What is the value of mutex, and how many processes are blocked?
options: 0, with one process blocked.
−2, with two processes blocked.
1, with no process blocked.
−1, with two processes blocked.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The same decrement-then-test rule applies to a binary semaphore; only its permitted values on the way up are bounded by its use as a mutex.

Step by step.

  1. Initial value 1. A executes P: 1 → 0, and A continues because the value was positive before the decrement.
  2. B executes P: 0 → −1, and B blocks.
  3. C executes P: −1 → −2, and C blocks.
  4. After B the value is −1 and after C it is −2; the magnitude 2 is exactly the number of waiters.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) stops counting after the first waiter.
  • (B) double-counts by decrementing once for the holder as well.
  • (C) ignores the two blocked calls entirely.

Common misconception. A binary semaphore's value is binary only while it is non-negative. Once waiters queue up, the value goes negative and counts them.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about semaphore values and semaphore operations are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Blocking inside P rather than spinning avoids wasting a processor while the process waits.
A counting semaphore initialised to 0, with no blocked process, means that no unit of the resource is currently available.
If P were not executed atomically, two processes could both observe a positive value and both decrement it, so mutual exclusion would fail.
A counting semaphore initialised to 5 gives mutual exclusion for a critical section in exactly the same way as one initialised to 1.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A semaphore is a counter plus an atomic decrement-or-block and an atomic increment-or-wake.

Step by step.

  1. The wait queue is the point of the construct: the waiting process is descheduled instead of burning cycles.
  2. The initial value is the number of permits, so 0 permits means every unit is in use.
  3. The atomicity of P is what prevents the lost-update race between two decrements.
  4. A semaphore initialised to 5 admits five processes into the section at once, which is the opposite of mutual exclusion.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (D) is the statement to reject: the initial value must be 1 for the semaphore to act as a mutex.

Common misconception. The initial value is not decoration — it is the admission count. Only 1 gives mutual exclusion.

questions.question: One implementation of P and V disables interrupts while the semaphore value is tested and updated, which makes the pair atomic on a uniprocessor. On a multiprocessor the same implementation is unsafe because:
options: disabling interrupts is illegal while a process is in user mode, so P and V could never be called.
the interrupt mask is per processor, so another processor can execute P on the same semaphore at the same instant and the update is no longer atomic.
disabling interrupts makes P and V take unbounded time, which breaks bounded waiting.
the semaphore value is held in a register rather than in memory, so the mask does not protect it.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An interrupt mask stops local preemption; it says nothing about another processor running in parallel.

Step by step.

  1. On a uniprocessor, disabling interrupts prevents any other process from being scheduled in the middle of the update, which is enough for atomicity.
  2. On a multiprocessor, the other processors keep running with their own masks, so two P operations can still interleave.
  3. The correct primitive is an atomic instruction (test-and-set, swap, compare-and-swap) on the semaphore's word, or a spin lock around the update.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is a privilege question, not the atomicity question being asked.
  • (C) is a timing concern, not a correctness one.
  • (D) is false: the semaphore is a shared memory word.

Common misconception. Interrupt masking is the standard uniprocessor answer and the standard multiprocessor mistake. The mask is local to one processor.

questions.question: In the bounded-buffer producer–consumer problem with capacity N, the counting semaphore full counts the items in the buffer and empty counts the free slots. A producer blocks when:
options: full = 0.
empty = 0.
mutex = 0.
empty = N.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The producer consumes a free slot before it produces; it blocks when no free slot is left.

Step by step.

  1. The producer executes P(empty) before inserting and V(full) after.
  2. It can only block inside P(empty), which happens when empty has reached 0.
  3. At that instant the buffer holds N items, so full = N as well; the two statements describe the same state, which is why only one of them appears in the options.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the state in which a consumer blocks.
  • (C) means another process is inside the buffer update.
  • (D) is the initial state, with an empty buffer.

Common misconception. Swapping the two semaphores is the classic bug: a producer that waits on full blocks as soon as the buffer is empty, which is exactly when it should be producing.

questions.question: In the second readers–writers solution, a writer that arrives while readers are active blocks new readers from entering. The main hazard of this solution is that:
options: two writers can enter the shared data at the same time.
readers and writers can deadlock on the shared mutex.
a reader can be kept waiting indefinitely while new writers keep arriving.
readers can no longer read concurrently with one another.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Giving writers priority removes writer starvation by creating reader starvation.

Step by step.

  1. When a writer is waiting, arriving readers are made to queue behind it, so writers are served promptly.
  2. If writers arrive continuously, each new writer re-blocks the readers before the previous queue drains.
  3. A reader can therefore wait without any bound, which is starvation rather than deadlock — the system keeps making progress, just not for that reader.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (B) are prevented by the writer mutex and the read-count protocol.
  • (D) is false: the first reader still holds the mutex on behalf of all readers, so readers continue to share the data.

Common misconception. The two readers–writers solutions are mirror images: the first starves writers, the second starves readers. Neither is 'the correct one' without a stated priority policy.

questions.question: In the dining-philosophers problem with five philosophers and five forks, the solution that admits at most four philosophers to compete for forks at any time prevents deadlock. Which one of the following is the reason?
options: Four philosophers cannot all be hungry at the same time, so contention disappears.
The fifth philosopher permanently holds the extra fork, which breaks the cycle.
It removes the mutual-exclusion requirement on the forks.
With at most four competitors for five forks, at least one philosopher can always obtain both neighbours' forks, so the circular-wait condition cannot hold.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions; the four-at-a-time rule removes circular wait.

Step by step.

  1. If each of four philosophers held one fork, that accounts for four of the five forks.
  2. The fifth fork is free and belongs to one of those four philosophers as its second fork, so that philosopher can pick it up and eat.
  3. Eating releases both forks, which lets the others proceed in turn; a cycle in which every philosopher waits for a neighbour can therefore never close.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is false: hunger has nothing to do with the bound.
  • (B) invents a fork that does not exist.
  • (C) is false: each fork is still used by one philosopher at a time.

Common misconception. The bound is not about politeness; it is a structural argument that some philosopher always has both forks available. Without that argument the rule looks arbitrary.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the classic synchronisation problems are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The dining-philosophers problem with one fork between neighbours models both deadlock and starvation.
The first readers–writers solution allows several readers to be inside the shared data at the same time.
A monitor is a semaphore with an associated counter of the processes waiting on it.
With counting semaphores full and empty in a bounded buffer of capacity N, the relation full + empty = N holds at every instant.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each of these three statements is a standard structural fact about the classical problems.

Step by step.

  1. Dining philosophers: if every philosopher picks up the left fork first, all five can hold one fork and wait for ever — deadlock; a philosopher can also be overtaken indefinitely — starvation.
  2. First readers–writers: the first reader takes the mutex, later readers only increment a count, so readers share the data concurrently.
  3. In the bounded buffer every slot is either full or empty, so the two counters always sum to the capacity.
  4. A monitor is a language-level construct with mutual exclusion built in plus condition variables; it is not a semaphore with a counter.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) is the statement to reject: condition variables and semaphores are different primitives, and a monitor is a module, not a counter.

Common misconception. Monitors are often introduced right after semaphores, which invites the idea that one is a renamed version of the other. They differ in where the mutual exclusion lives.

questions.question: A bounded buffer has capacity 8 and is managed with the counting semaphores full and empty. At some instant full = 3 and no process is blocked. What is the value of empty?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every slot of the buffer is either occupied or free, so the two counters partition the capacity.

Step by step.

  1. The capacity is N = 8.
  2. Three slots hold items, so full = 3.
  3. The remaining slots are free: empty = N - full = 8 - 3 = 5.

Answer: 5.

Common misconception. Reporting 3 by symmetry with full, or 8 by treating empty as the capacity.

questions.question: Five philosophers sit around a circular table with one fork between each pair of neighbours, and the solution admits at most four philosophers to compete for forks at any instant. What is the maximum number of philosophers that can be eating at the same instant?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each eater needs two distinct forks, and a table of five has five forks.

Step by step.

  1. Two eaters use four forks and cannot be adjacent, because neighbours would share a fork.
  2. Three eaters would need six forks, which the table does not have.
  3. The bound is therefore ⌊5 / 2⌋ = 2, and it is achievable: philosophers 1 and 3 eat while 2, 4 and 5 wait.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Answering 4 by reading the four-at-a-time rule as a count of eaters rather than of competitors.

questions.question: Which one of the following is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for a deadlock to occur?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Each is necessary, and deadlock requires all four to hold at the same time.

Step by step.

  1. Mutual exclusion: at least one resource must be held in a non-shareable mode, so a second requester must wait.
  2. Hold and wait: a process must be holding at least one resource while it waits for another.
  3. No preemption: a resource can be released only voluntarily, by the process that holds it.
  4. Circular wait: there is a closed chain of processes in which each waits for a resource held by the next.
  5. Option (C) states the negation of the third condition. Deadlock needs preemption to be impossible, so “preemption of resources” is not a condition — it is the escape route.

Answer: Option (C) — preemption of resources is the opposite of the required condition, which is no preemption.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Mutual exclusion is the first Coffman condition.
  • (B) Hold and wait is the second.
  • (D) Circular wait is the fourth.

Common misconception. Many candidates tick “preemption” because the word does appear in the standard list. The list says no preemption: if the system could preempt a resource from a waiting process, the wait could never be permanent.

Takeaway. All four conditions must hold simultaneously. Denying any one of them makes deadlock impossible — that is exactly what deadlock prevention does.
options: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
Preemption of resources
Circular wait

questions.question: A resource allocation graph contains exactly one instance of every resource type. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. When every resource type has a single instance, each resource node has at most one outgoing edge, so the graph collapses into a wait-for graph on processes. In that graph deadlock and cycle are the same thing.

Step by step.

  1. Merge each resource node with its holder: draw Pᵢ → Pⱼ exactly when Pᵢ is waiting for a resource held by Pⱼ.
  2. Deadlock ⇒ cycle. If a set of processes is deadlocked, each member waits for a resource held by another member; following the waits around the set closes a cycle.
  3. Cycle ⇒ deadlock. Take a cycle P₁ → P₂ → … → Pₖ → P₁. Each Pᵢ waits for the single instance held by its successor, and that successor cannot release it, because it is itself waiting. No member can ever proceed.
  4. Hence with single instances the cycle test is a complete decision procedure.

Answer: Option (B) — with one instance per resource type, a cycle is necessary and sufficient for deadlock.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the correct statement only when a resource type may have several instances.
  • (C) reverses the quantifiers: a deadlock always contains a cycle, so a cycle cannot be merely sufficient.
  • (D) denies a standard theorem.

Common misconception. Candidates learn “cycle is necessary, not sufficient” as a slogan and apply it everywhere. That slogan belongs to the multi-instance case; with single instances the cycle test decides.

Takeaway. Single instance → wait-for graph → cycle test. Multiple instances → graph reduction.
options: A cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock.
A cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock.
A cycle is sufficient but not necessary for deadlock.
A cycle is neither necessary nor sufficient for deadlock.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the difference between deadlock and starvation?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Deadlock is a closed failure: every member of the blocked set waits for a member of that same set, so nobody can be released. Starvation is an open failure: the system as a whole progresses, but the allocation policy repeatedly passes one process over.

Step by step.

  1. In deadlock, the blocked set is closed under waiting — each process's requested resource is held by another blocked member — so no member can ever be unblocked.
  2. In starvation, other processes acquire and release the contended resource all the time; only the victim is never selected.
  3. A cycle in the wait-for graph is the signature of deadlock, not of starvation: a starving process has no cycle, only a policy that ignores it.
  4. Therefore the distinguishing feature is whether the rest of the system progresses.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the facts: a cycle accompanies deadlock, and starvation needs no cycle.
  • (C) describes no real property of either condition.
  • (D) confuses the resource conditions with the scheduling failure.

Common misconception. The two terms are often used as synonyms. A system can be completely deadlock-free and still starve a low-priority process forever.

Takeaway. Deadlock: nobody progresses. Starvation: everybody except one progresses. Cure deadlock by breaking a wait cycle; cure starvation by aging or fair queueing.
options: In deadlock a set of processes waits forever for resources held by one another; in starvation one process waits indefinitely while the other processes keep making progress.
Starvation always leaves a cycle in the wait-for graph, while deadlock never does.
Deadlock ends as soon as the highest-priority process finishes, while starvation can never end.
Starvation requires mutual exclusion, while deadlock does not.

questions.question: Deadlock avoidance differs from deadlock prevention in that avoidance:
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The three strategies are distinct. Prevention removes a Coffman condition at design time. Avoidance keeps every condition intact but refuses any allocation that would leave the system without a safe completion order, using each process's declared maximum. Detection lets deadlock happen and then finds it.

Step by step.

  1. Prevention acts on structure: request all resources at once (denies hold and wait), or number the resources (denies circular wait).
  2. Avoidance acts on decisions: every request is granted only if the resulting state is still safe. This needs each process's maximum claim in advance, which is why it is a runtime technique.
  3. Avoidance denies none of the four conditions — processes still hold, still wait, still exclude. It only refuses allocations that could lead to deadlock.
  4. So the distinguishing feature is the use of future maximum claims to maintain safety.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the definition of prevention.
  • (C) is detection followed by recovery.
  • (D) describes no real strategy: waiting is normal even in a deadlock-free system.

Common misconception. Banker's algorithm is often filed under “prevention”. It is avoidance: the four conditions still hold, but the system never enters an unsafe state.

Takeaway. Prevention removes a condition; avoidance never enters an unsafe state; detection finds and breaks. Three strategies, three different guarantees.
options: structurally denies one of the four necessary conditions, so deadlock becomes impossible by construction
uses advance information about each process's future maximum claims to keep the system in a safe state
detects cycles in the resource allocation graph and rolls processes back
guarantees that no process ever waits for a resource

questions.question: A system state is called safe when:
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Safety is defined by the existence of a safe sequence: an order in which every process can be given its full remaining claim, run to completion and release everything, so that the next process in the order can do the same.

Step by step.

  1. Start from the current Available vector.
  2. Repeatedly look for a process whose remaining Need ≤ Available. Let it finish and add its whole allocation back to Available.
  3. If all processes can be finished this way, the state is safe and the order found is a safe sequence.
  4. Safety is a worst-case guarantee: if every process requests at most its declared maximum, a safe state can never deadlock, because the safe sequence always has a next step available.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) A state in which processes wait can still be safe; waiting is not deadlock.
  • (C) That is the opposite extreme — every process has already taken everything it may take.
  • (D) Acyclicity is a property of single-instance graphs; it is neither the definition of safety nor equivalent to it.

Common misconception. “Unsafe” is read as “deadlocked”. Unsafe means only that no safe sequence exists at this instant, so deadlock has become possible; the processes may still finish if they request less than their maximum.

Takeaway. Safe ⊂ deadlock-free. Unsafe ⊇ deadlocked. The two inclusions are strict.
options: no process is currently waiting for a resource

there exists an ordering of all processes in which each process's remaining maximum demand can be met from the currently available resources plus the resources released by the processes that precede it in that ordering
every process's current allocation equals its declared maximum
the resource allocation graph contains no cycle

questions.question:
A system has two resource types: R₁ with 2 instances and R₂ with 1 instance. Three processes hold and request them as follows.
Allocated : R₁ → P1 , R₁ → P2 , R₂ → P3
Requested : P1 → R₂ , P2 → R₂ , P3 → R₁
Which of the following statements about the current state is TRUE?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With more than one instance per resource type a cycle is only a necessary condition, so the verdict comes from graph reduction: repeatedly let a process whose outstanding request can be met finish, and add all of its resources back to the pool.

Step by step.

  1. Compute what is free. R₁: 2 − 2 = 0 available. R₂: 1 − 1 = 0 available.
  2. P1 and P2 both request R₂, whose only instance is held by P3. P3 requests R₁, whose two instances are held by P1 and P2.
  3. No process's request can be satisfied from the available pool, so no process can finish and no edge can be removed. Reduction stalls immediately.
  4. The processes left behind wait only on one another, so they are deadlocked. The cycle is P1 → R₂ → P3 → R₁ → P1.

Answer: Option (A) — the graph cannot be reduced, so the system is deadlocked.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Two instances in total is irrelevant once both are already allocated; the free count is zero.
  • (C) Holding one resource each is exactly the arrangement that closes the cycle.
